before: class FramedLabel(Label) makes Label a base class. FramedLabel inherits its initializer and can replace render with its own implementation. Creating FramedLabel("Map") therefore still initializes self.text on that new instance.

Inside the overriding render method, super() returns a proxy for continuing method lookup after the current class. Calling .render() on that proxy reaches Label.render in this single-inheritance example, with the same instance. It is not a new Label object and does not mean "call every parent".

after:
A class can reuse another class's methods. This is called inheritance.

In `class FramedLabel(Label):`, `Label` is the base class we build on. `FramedLabel` reuses its setup method and gives `render` a new version. This replacement is called overriding.

`FramedLabel("Map")` still saves `"Map"` as the new object's `self.text`.

Inside `FramedLabel.render`, `super().render()` looks for the next `render` method after `FramedLabel` in Python's class order. Here it finds `Label.render`.

Both methods work on the same object. `super()` does not create another `Label`, and it does not call every parent class.

Using `self.render()` here would call `FramedLabel.render` again. That method would keep calling itself. With no stopping rule, Python eventually raises `RecursionError`.

Use `super().render()` to reach the next method instead.

Keep `Label`'s setup and `render` methods. Complete `FramedLabel.render` with `super()`.

For extra practice, make another class based on `Label` that adds a different decoration. Check that a plain `Label` still returns its original text.
